# Lessons From The Version 3 Slip

My write-up of why Quaylane 3.0 shipped on 2026-09-15 instead of 2026-06-23, for the engineering meeting of 2026-11-04. Not a postmortem in the incident sense; nobody did anything wrong except the plan, and I wrote the plan.

## What happened

- 2026-01-05: scope and date set at [[version-3-scope-meeting-2026-01-05]] on the assumption of all five engineers on product work from March, plus the first 2026 hire from April.
- February to May: the [[tenant-isolation-migration]] ran past its pilot and the [[reminder-outage-2026-03-17]] added nine postmortem actions. Teodora and Kwabena spent 11 weeks on that work instead of product.
- 2026-05-12: I asked whether SSO should be split from 3.0 ([[should-v3-ship-without-sso]]), worried about the wrong feature.
- 2026-06-02: date moved, SSO split out ([[release-planning-2026-06-02]]).

## What I think we learned

1. **The plan had no slack for platform work with no end date.** The tenant migration was open-ended by nature. I treated its pilot end date as a project end date.
2. **I noticed in March and did not act.** After the outage I knew two engineers were gone for weeks. I should have moved the date in April, when it would have cost one round of customer emails instead of a month of them.
3. **Only one date was protected, and it held.** SSO had a contract, an owner and slack. That is the model for any date we promise ([[dates-are-promises-only-when-contractual]]).
4. **The people closest to the work called it right.** Lucia said in April that calendars were behind. I heard it as normal mid-project worry.

## What we changed

- Roadmap themes have appetites, not dates ([[appetite-based-scoping]]).
- A fixed 30% platform reservation in the 2027 capacity plan.
- Customer-facing dates only inside six weeks or when contractual ([[should-release-dates-be-promised-to-customers]]).
- The release train belongs to Lucia, who sees slippage earlier than I do.

## What I am not concluding

That we should not have done the tenant work. It was needed for Meridale and for every security conversation since. The mistake was pretending it was free.
